title: The Amos and Andy film in Hollywood
summary: Making the Amos and Andy picture was exciting for a band that was among the first to appear in film.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah. Okay. Well, I think maybe you did make that first film, sometime. Maybe in '30 or '31. The Amos and Andy film, do you think?
Well what was that like? Going out to Hollywood and --
Yeah. It really was very exciting to
us. Going to Hollywood to make a picture, a movie with Amos and Andy. That was very big for us.
Well, I mean, actually, I don't think any jazz bands -- well, maybe Whiteman had been in a film. But I don't think any other jazz bands had been, had they?
I don't know. I don't think so.
But it was very, very exciting to us to be working with Amos and Andy.
Yeah. It must have been terrific. And then like shooting the sequences and everything, did they -- I mean was it dubbed, or how was it done? Was it recorded live, or how was it done? Do you remember?
Because they couldn't have had -- the equipment wasn't the same in those days. I think you had to -- I think they got the music down, and then you had to go through it.
I believe. I think that's how it was.
And then you had some very good picture calls, remember? There were some very good band pictures out of that period.
It was a very exciting time.
Yeah. Well, that was good. That was wonderful. Well, everything for the band was going very big then. Because it was one thing after another. The records were going very big.
And I guess Duke was writing a lot of hits.

Although, I don't think he'd written -- I don't think he had the big hits then -- by then. I don't think he had "Mood Indigo" or "Sophisticated Lady". They hadn't been written then, I don't think. Had they?
No, I don't think so. A little later on, it was, I think.
